Judgment
Amal Ranaraja. J,
1. The accused-appellant (hereinafter referred to as the ‘appellant’) has
been indicted in the High Court of Kuliyapitiya in Case No.
HC/029/2019. The charges in the indictment are as follows;
01. That between the period of the 01st of January, 2013 and the
15th of February, 2013, within the jurisdiction of this Court,
in Dikirikawe Panapitiya, you in order to gain some sexual
gratification have used a certain part of your body on one
Rajapaksha Suriya Bandara Arachchilage Rachini Shalika, a
person under 16 years of age, i.e. by rubbing your male
genitalia in between her legs; thereby you have committed an
offence of “Grave Sexual Abuse” punishable under Section
365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka as amended by
Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.22 of 1995, Penal Code
(Amendment) Act No. 29 of 1998 and Penal Code (Amendment)
Act No. 16 of 2006.
02. That between the period of the 01st of January, 2013 and the
15th of February, 2013, at a separate occasion than that of the
above first charge, within the jurisdiction of this Court, in
Dikirikawe Panapitiya, you in order to gain some sexual
gratification have used a certain part of your body on one
Rajapaksha Suriya Bandara Arachchilage Rachini Shalika, a
person under 16 years of age, i.e. by rubbing your male
genitalia in between her legs; thereby you have committed an
offence of “Grave Sexual Abuse” punishable under Section
365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka as amended by
Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.22 of 1995, Penal Code
(Amendment) Act No. 29 of 1998 and Penal Code (Amendment)
Act No. 16 of 2006.
03. That on or around the 16th of February, 2013, at the location
mentioned in the above first charge, you in order to gain some
sexual gratification have used a certain part of your body on
one Rajapaksha Suriya Bandara Arachchilage Rachini
Shalika, a person under 16 years of age, i.e. by rubbing your
male genitalia in between her legs; thereby you have
committed an offence of “Grave Sexual Abuse” punishable
under Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka as
amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.22 of 1995,
Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 1998 and Penal Code
(Amendment) Act No. 16 of 2006.
2. At the conclusion of the trial, the appellant has been convicted of the
first charge and acquitted of the second and the third charges. Upon
conviction the appellant has been sentenced as follows;
I. 7 years rigorous imprisonment and also has been imposed a fine
of Rs. 5000.00 with a term of 1 month simple imprisonment, in
default.
The appellant has also been directed to pay a sum of Rs.
100,000.00, as compensation to PW01 with a term of 1 year
simple imprisonment, in default.
Further, it has been directed that the term of 1 year simple
imprisonment in default, shall run consequent to the term of 7
years rigorous imprisonment.
Case of the Prosecution
3. PW01, born in October 2000, has lived in Dikirikawe Panapitiya, a town
located in the North-Western Province of Sri Lanka. She has attended
Mitiyagane Maha Vidyalaya and has been a year 7 student at that time.
She has resided with her parents and younger brother. Her
grandmother has also lived close by. Both her parents have been
employed and would return home after she and her brother came back
from school. It had been customary for her to complete her homework
upon returning from school. Afterwards, she and her brother would go
to their grandmother’s house until their parents returned from work.
4. On the day of the incident, PW01 and her brother have returned from
school. The brother had then left home to attend extra lessons, leaving
PW01 alone. At that time, the appellant, who was known to PW01 and
employed by her grandmother to clear an adjacent property has come
by and requested some water to drink. PW01 has obliged.
5. Thereafter, PW01 has returned to her room. The appellant has allegedly
followed her, subsequently, threatened her with a knife, has committed
sexual abuse as detailed in the first charge, i.e. engaged in intercrural
sex with PW01 against her will.
6. PW01 has shared the incident with a school friend. In turn, the friend
has notified a teacher about what had happened. The teacher has then
questioned PW01, who has provided a written explanation of the
incident involving the appellant. This written explanation has been
submitted as evidence and marked පැ 02. Following a police complaint,
an investigation has commenced.
7. PW01 has subsequently been presented to Dr. A.P. Karagampitiya, a
medical officer attached to the outpatient department (OPD) of the
Teaching Hospital in Kurunegala. Upon examining PW01, Dr.
Karagampitiya has prepared a medico-legal report. This report has
produced as evidence and marked පැ 03.
Case of the Appellant
8. The appellant has denied the incidents described in the charges. He has
also denied offering money to PW01, asserting instead that he provided
funds to PW01’s brother for the purchase of books.
Grounds of appeal
9. When the matter was taken up for argument, the learned counsel
appearing on behalf of the appellant has urged the following grounds of
appeal;
I. Failure to apply the judicial caution required in assessing the
evidence of child witness when there is overwhelming evidence
against;
i. Contradictions per se and inter se pf the evidence of PW01
and PW04.
ii. Authenticity of the letter පැ 02 and signs of tutoring.
iii. Teacher’s conduct in channelling the complaint.
iv. Police investigators unduly and culpably interested in the
outcome.
v. Lack of corroborative value of medico-legal evidence and
the inability of ‘short history given by the patient’ to
determine consistency.
II. Failure to consider an alternative narrative arising from PW01’s
attainment of menarche.
III. Failure to consider investigative lapses, leading to material
irregularities and denial of fair trial.
10. The written explanation submitted to the designated teacher by PW01
been produced as evidence, marked පැ 02. The appellant has contended
that the structure of this explanation is beyond the capacity of a child
of PW01’s age. Accordingly, PW01 is alleged to have been coached before
drafting the contents of පැ 02 and the statement given to the
investigator.
11. A reading of පැ 02 shows that PW01 has expressed in simple language
the incident involving the appellant. For the convenience of those
relevant, I reproduce the contents of පැ 02;
Vide පැ 02 on Page 271 of the Brief
12. PW01 has explained the manner in which the appellant had attempted
to familiarise himself with her. She has then recounted how, on the date
of the incident, the appellant has come to her house, requested a glass
of water and subsequently, engaged in the sexual act with her under
threat.
13. The explanation provided is, as stated above in simple language,
avoiding any legal jargon to clarify the incident. Although the appellant
has argued that the structure of this explanation was beyond the
capacity or understanding of PW01, he has not elaborated on this point
in a convincing manner.
14. The capacity to explain an incident as well as the understanding and
structure of the explanation is relative. There is no single universal
method for doing so. The ability to express oneself clearly is crucial in
this context. There is no evidence that PW01 was incapable of
expressing herself as demonstrated in of පැ 02. Hence, the contention
that PW01 has been coached before drafting the contents of පැ 02 and
the statement given to the investigator must fail.
15. The appellant has also argued that there are significant discrepancies
in the testimony of witnesses, PW01 and PW04 as well in the statements
they provided to the investigator. Consequently, the appellant asserts
that this inconsistency calls into question the reliability of their
testimonies, suggesting they should not be used as the basis for
convicting the appellant of the charges faced.
16. Marking a contradiction, in a witness’s testimony is a core cross-
examination technique used to impeach credibility. It involves
confronting a witness with his own prior inconsistent statements (such
as a previous police statement) to expose irreconcilable differences in
his account. Confronting and impeaching a witness by such technique
(the marking step) involves the following; the witness’s attention is to be
drawn to the exact part of the previous statement that contradicts his
current testimony. Quote the specific lines from the prior recorded
statement. Ask the witness to explain why his previous statement differs
from his current testimony. If the witness denies making the previous
statement, the cross examining attorney will officially mark that
specific, inconsistent portion of the previous statement as a Court
exhibit. The investigating officer or the person who recorded the
statement will later be called to prove it was actually made.
17. In the case of Agampodi Wijepala de Soyza vs Officer in Charge,
Ahungalla and Another SC Appeal 159/2018, decided on 07.07.2021, P.
Padman Surasena J (as he was then), has held as follows,
“Moreover, the Evidence Ordinance in section 145 specifically provides
for the manner in which a witness can be cross-examined and
confronted with the statements made by such witness previously and
the procedure to be adopted when proving such statements. It is
worthwhile to reproduce here the said section.
Section 145.
(1) A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements
made by him in writing or reduced into writing and relevant
to matters in question without such writing being shown to
him or being proved; but if it is intended to contradict him
by the writing, his attention must, before the writing can be
proved, be called to those parts of it which are to be used for
the purpose of contradicting him.
(2) If a witness, upon cross examination as to a previous oral
statement made by him relevant to matters in question in the
suit or proceeding in which he is cross examined and
inconsistent with his present testimony, does not distinctly
admit that he made such statement, proof may be given that
he did in fact make it; but before such proof can be given the
circumstances of the supposed statement sufficient to
designate the particular occasion must be mentioned to the
witness, and he must be asked whether or not he made such
a statement
The scheme of the above section clearly demands that the following
mandatory steps must be adhered to, when marking and proving an
inconsistency.
Firstly, a cross-examining counsel who intends to show that the
evidence of the witness under cross examination is contradictory with a
previous statement made by him, must ask questions relevant to such
matters in question without such previous statements being shown to
him.
Secondly, if such witness comes out with something that is prima facie
inconsistent with any part of such statement, it is then only the section
allows such counsel to bring such parts of such statement which are to
be used for the purpose of contradicting him, to the attention of such
witness.
Thirdly, if such witness has stated something inconsistent with his
previous statement and does not distinctly admit making such previous
statement, then the cross-examining counsel is under a duty as per
subsection 2 of the above section to ask whether or not such witness has
made such a previous statement.
Fourthly, it is thereafter only the cross-examining counsel can proceed
to prove that such witness has in fact made such previous statement.”
18. However, trivial, minor inconsistencies, rarely impact the core of the
case. To successfully discredit a witness, the contradiction must be
material to a key fact in the issue.
19. In the case of Bandara Vs. The State (2001) 1 SLR 63, Kulathilake J, has
stated,
“Our Courts have laid down the principle that the discrepancies
and inconsistencies which do not relate to the core of prosecution
case ought to be disregarded especially when all probabilities
factor echoes in favour of the version narrated by a witness.”
20. PW01 has testified to the events described in the first charge. While the
appellant has contended that PW01’s testimony contains discrepancies,
such discrepancies have not been established as noted elsewhere in the
judgement.
21. In her history provided to Dr. A.P. Karagampitiya, Medical Officer, PW01
has stated as follows;
Vide Page 11 of the Case Brief
Accordingly, she has remained consistent in that regard. The testimony
of PW01 has been cogent and convincing.
22. The appellant has also sought to undermine the credibility of PW01’s
testimony by alleging that her account included a penile-vaginal
penetration involving the appellant and the credibility of such testimony
is not supported by the absence of evidence that PW01 had attained
menarche at the time.
23. Menarche is a girl’s first menstrual period, making the biological
capacity for reproduction. Penile-vaginal penetration is physically
possible before menarche because, the reproduction organs are present.
The vaginal canal exists and can allow penetration but, it carries severe
risks of physical trauma and emotional harm.
24. Research suggests that child witnesses often exhibit a tendency to
exaggerate when recounting events. This phenomenon can be attributed
to a variety of factors, including psychological development of children,
their emotional responses to traumatic events and the influence of
external circumstances.
25. Children perceive and interpret the world differently. Their
understanding of events particularly those that are distressing or
frightening can be influenced by their imagination and emotional state.
In moments of anxiety or fear, a child’s instinct may lead them to distort
experiences as a coping mechanism. This natural inclination to
exaggerate can stem from their attempts to make sense of overwhelming
situations, adding unnecessary details to their accounts to echo with
what they perceive as the seriousness of the event.
26. Children are also often eager to please adults and may feel pressure to
conform to perceived expectations. This pressure can lead them to
exaggerate their accounts in an attempt to create a narrative that aligns
with what they believe others want to hear.
27. Children’s memories are also easily influenced by suggestions,
discussions with family members or others of similar events. Such
factors may result in distortions and exaggerations as children attempt
to reconstruct memories that are not entirely accurate. Further,
traumatic events in particular can provoke strong feelings, resulting in
vivid recollections but these memories may not always reflect factual
accuracy. The intensity of emotions can blur the lines of reality for
young witnesses, prompting them to recount experiences with dramatic
flair even if such exaggeration diverges from actual events.
28. Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance of Sri Lanka is as follows;
“134. No particular number of witnesses shall in any case be required
for the proof of any fact.”
29. The law focuses on the weight and credibility of testimony rather than
counting witnesses. A court can base a judgement or conviction on the
uncorroborated testimony of a single witness if the judge believes it.
Courts do not need multiple witnesses to verify a single event or fact.
30. In the decided case of Sumanasena vs Attorney General 1999 3 SLR 137,
Jayasuriya J, has stated,
“Evidence must not be counted but weighed and the evidence of a single
solitary witness if cogent and impressive could be acted upon by a Court
of law.”
Consequently, the learned High Court Judge was correct in considering
the testimony of PW01 and acting upon it. It also contradicts the claim
that the investigators have not performed a proper investigation, given
their failure to record relevant witnesses.
31. In those circumstances, I am not inclined to interfere with the
conviction, disputed judgement together with the sentencing order and
proceed to affirm the same. The term of 7 years rigorous imprisonment
shall commence from the date the instant judgement is read and
explained to the appellant in the High Court of Kuliyapitiya.
32. I dismiss the appeal but make no order regarding costs.
Appeal dismissed.
33. The Registrar of this Court is directed to send this Judgement to the
High Court in Kuliyapitiya for compliance.
